title: Bidirectional BFS in Reykjavík: Find the route fast!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS visualize how two search frontiers meet in the middle to dramatically cut exploration on a street graph. From start to finish, every wave expands level-by-level—then snaps to the shortest path when the frontiers collide.
ig_caption:
🌍✨ Reykjavík (Miðborg) street-map vibes, but with real graph theory.

🔍 Bidirectional BFS works by launching two BFS searches simultaneously—one from the start node and one from the goal node—on the same unweighted road-graph model. Each BFS expands in “layers” (same-distance hops), and the moment the visited sets intersect, we reconstruct the shortest route with far fewer node expansions than a one-direction BFS.

📌 In graph terms: you’re reducing search depth from O(b^d) to roughly O(b^(d/2)) (typical branching factor b, solution depth d) by meeting in the middle—perfect for shortest-path problems on grid-like or road-adjacent maps.

🗺️ This visualization treats intersections/waypoints as vertices and road segments as edges, then runs Bidirectional BFS over that graph derived from real-world geography.

👉 Want a version on your city? Drop your city + the two landmarks to route between in the comments, and I’ll generate a visualization prompt!
fb_caption:
🧠🚗 Testing shortest-path thinking on a real street graph from Reykjavík (Miðborg)! Bidirectional BFS uses two simultaneous breadth-first searches—one from the start and one from the goal—until their frontiers meet. That “meet-in-the-middle” strategy reduces how many intersections we explore while still guaranteeing the shortest path on an unweighted graph.
